claims.claim: **The most common cause in adolescents is anovulatory cycles.** ⚠️ **Important differentials: bleeding disorders and pregnancy-related bleeding.**
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Adolescent gynaecology - heavy menstrual bleeding' (Last updated June 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Adolescent_Gynaecology_Menorrhagia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Excessive flow** = more than 7 days or more than 80 mL per cycle · changing a super pad/tampon more often than every 2 hours · symptomatic anaemia · lifestyle disturbance.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Adolescent gynaecology - heavy menstrual bleeding' (Last updated June 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Adolescent_Gynaecology_Menorrhagia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Causes to consider:** pregnancy (miscarriage, ectopic, gestational trophoblastic disease); **von Willebrand disease**, platelet function disorder, thrombocytopenia; thyroid dysfunction, PCOS; hormonal contraception and anticoagulants.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Adolescent gynaecology - heavy menstrual bleeding' (Last updated June 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Adolescent_Gynaecology_Menorrhagia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Severity:** mild — slightly or moderately increased flow, normal haemoglobin · moderate — menses every 1–3 weeks, moderate–heavy flow, haemoglobin reduced but at least 100 g/L · ⚠️ **severe — haemoglobin under 100 g/L and/or haemodynamic instability.**
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Adolescent gynaecology - heavy menstrual bleeding' (Last updated June 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Adolescent_Gynaecology_Menorrhagia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **An adolescent rarely needs a vaginal examination**; discuss with a senior clinician, and if needed perform it only once.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Adolescent gynaecology - heavy menstrual bleeding' (Last updated June 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Adolescent_Gynaecology_Menorrhagia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Consider FBE, ferritin, coagulation screen, TSH and βhCG (with consent)**; group and hold if bleeding is severe.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Adolescent gynaecology - heavy menstrual bleeding' (Last updated June 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Adolescent_Gynaecology_Menorrhagia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Suspected bleeding disorder: consider PFA-100 and a von Willebrand screen — not during acute bleeding or after recent NSAID use.**
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Adolescent gynaecology - heavy menstrual bleeding' (Last updated June 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Adolescent_Gynaecology_Menorrhagia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Pelvic ultrasound is rarely required** — only for atypical features or a palpable mass.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Adolescent gynaecology - heavy menstrual bleeding' (Last updated June 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Adolescent_Gynaecology_Menorrhagia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Mild:** if contraception is not wanted, reassure and observe; consider tranexamic acid and regular NSAIDs during menses. **Moderate:** tranexamic acid during menses, plus an oral progestogen-only or combined oral contraceptive pill.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Adolescent gynaecology - heavy menstrual bleeding' (Last updated June 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Adolescent_Gynaecology_Menorrhagia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Severe:** consider pregnancy or a bleeding disorder; resuscitation with IV access, tranexamic acid, and hormonal therapy (e.g. high-dose norethisterone); iron infusion, or packed red cells if haemodynamically unstable despite fluids; **gynaecology review and consider inpatient observation.**
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Adolescent gynaecology - heavy menstrual bleeding' (Last updated June 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Adolescent_Gynaecology_Menorrhagia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Consider iron supplementation** and a menstrual calendar or app.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Adolescent gynaecology - heavy menstrual bleeding' (Last updated June 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Adolescent_Gynaecology_Menorrhagia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Tranexamic acid 15–25 mg/kg (max 1 g) 2–3 times a day on heavy days** — cuts flow by 25–50%.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Adolescent gynaecology - heavy menstrual bleeding' (Last updated June 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Adolescent_Gynaecology_Menorrhagia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **NSAIDs taken regularly during menstruation** (e.g. naproxen 500 mg bd or mefenamic acid 500 mg tds) reduce flow and can be combined with tranexamic acid.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Adolescent gynaecology - heavy menstrual bleeding' (Last updated June 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Adolescent_Gynaecology_Menorrhagia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Active bleeding:** norethisterone 5–10 mg three times daily for 10 days, then wean slowly (e.g. by 5 mg/week) **or** medroxyprogesterone acetate 10–20 mg tds, 10 days, after which stop or continue 10 mg daily.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Adolescent gynaecology - heavy menstrual bleeding' (Last updated June 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Adolescent_Gynaecology_Menorrhagia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Abruptly stopping progestogen-only treatment will precipitate bleeding.** For non-response or higher doses, get specialist advice.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Adolescent gynaecology - heavy menstrual bleeding' (Last updated June 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Adolescent_Gynaecology_Menorrhagia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Prophylaxis options:** depot medroxyprogesterone acetate 150 mg every 12 weeks by IM injection · continuous norethisterone 5–10 mg daily or continuous medroxyprogesterone acetate 10 mg daily · Mirena LNG-IUD, replaced 5–8-yearly.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Adolescent gynaecology - heavy menstrual bleeding' (Last updated June 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Adolescent_Gynaecology_Menorrhagia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **The COC can cut flow by 50%**; usually start low-dose oestrogen with moderate progestin (e.g. ethinylestradiol 30 microg + levonorgestrel 150 microg). Check contraindications.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Adolescent gynaecology - heavy menstrual bleeding' (Last updated June 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Adolescent_Gynaecology_Menorrhagia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Active bleeding:** take one pill eight-hourly until the bleeding stops (usually within 48 hours) → a pill 12-hourly for 3 days → one a day continuously until outpatient review.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Adolescent gynaecology - heavy menstrual bleeding' (Last updated June 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Adolescent_Gynaecology_Menorrhagia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Prophylaxis:** one pill daily; once the first month's withdrawal bleed has happened, switch to continuous use.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Adolescent gynaecology - heavy menstrual bleeding' (Last updated June 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Adolescent_Gynaecology_Menorrhagia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **GP or paediatrician review in 2 weeks** to confirm active bleeding has resolved; after starting maintenance, **review in 3–4 months.**
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Adolescent gynaecology - heavy menstrual bleeding' (Last updated June 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Adolescent_Gynaecology_Menorrhagia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Involve gynaecology for:** severe bleeding · haemodynamic instability · symptomatic anaemia · haemoglobin under 100 g/L · no response to tranexamic acid and/or hormonal treatment.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Adolescent gynaecology - heavy menstrual bleeding' (Last updated June 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Adolescent_Gynaecology_Menorrhagia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Discharge when stable with review booked:** mild bleeding within a month, **ongoing heavy bleeding within 48 hours.**
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Adolescent gynaecology - heavy menstrual bleeding' (Last updated June 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Adolescent_Gynaecology_Menorrhagia/, retrieved 2026-09-23
